source: Stanford Encyclopedia: Epistemology of Disagreement (Christensen, Elga, Kelly, Lackey positions)
finding: Equal Weight view rests on three claims: Defeat, Equal Weight, Independence. Independence says you may not discount a peer using reasons drawn from the disputed matter itself.
numbers: Restaurant Check case: credences 0.7 and 0.3 both move to 0.5.
quote: Learning that a peer disagrees with you about P gives you a reason to believe you are mistaken about P.
limits: Philosophical argument, no data. Conciliationism may undermine itself when experts disagree about it. Only the first 100000 characters read.
agent_relevance: Independence is the formal source of G4: a peer only counts as a peer if its error is not tied to yours. Copies of one model are not independent peers.

source: SEP: steadfast, justificationist and total-evidence replies to conciliationism
finding: Rivals reject one of the three claims: Right Reasons (first-order evidence only), Justificationist (Lackey: strong prior justification lets you demote a peer), Total Evidence (Kelly: bootstrapping case shows splitting the difference can lock in a wrong credence).
numbers: Kelly bootstrapping: two parties both misread evidence and split the difference to a wrong credence.
limits: The entry says peers are rare and shared background (same school, region) can lower the weight of an opinion.
agent_relevance: Shared training is shared background. This argues for down-weighting same-model samples, and for not averaging when all samples misread the same evidence.

source: Lorenz, Rauhut, Schweitzer, Helbing (2011) How social influence can undermine the wisdom of crowd effect
finding: Showing people others' estimates shrank diversity without improving accuracy, and raised confidence. Three effects: social influence, range reduction, confidence.
numbers: N=144 ETH students, 12 sessions of 12, 6 estimation questions, 5 rounds each. Arithmetic mean beat individual first estimates in only 21.3% of cases (77.1% on log scale). Range-reduction indicator about one unit lower with information than control.
limits: Moderate-difficulty questions only. Collective error fell slightly in the aggregated condition (mean drifts toward truth). No competition, authority or opinion questions. Small groups, student sample.
agent_relevance: Human precedent: reading peers' answers collapses variance. Sampling several answers and letting them read each other removes the independence that makes votes work.

source: Becker, Brackbill, Centola (2017) Network dynamics of social influence in the wisdom of crowds
finding: Counter-finding: in decentralized networks of 40, social influence improved accuracy. In centralized networks it helped or hurt depending on whether the hub was right.
numbers: N=1360 (1040 networked, 320 control). Decentralized: diversity -43%, individual error -23%, median error 0.76 to 0.67 SD (-12%), mean error 0.69 to 0.62 SD (-10%). Centralized: hub right, mean error -43%; hub wrong, mean error +19%, median +32%. Control: diversity -3%, no change.
limits: Numeric estimation tasks online. Self-weight correlated with accuracy (rho=0.41, n=4340). Large-group claim is a prediction. Authors say earlier small-group studies were underpowered.
agent_relevance: Influence helps only if accurate members hold their ground and no single node dominates. A single judge or lead agent is a hub: it helps only when it is right.

source: Mahmoodi et al. (2015) Equality bias impairs collective decision-making across cultures
finding: Dyads gave nearly equal weight to each other regardless of true competence. Better member overweighted, worse member underweighted. Persisted across cultures, feedback, noise and money.
numbers: Exp1: 98 men, 49 dyads (Denmark 15, Iran 15, China 19). Equal weight vs optimal t(93)=-4.19. Exp2 feedback 11 dyads; Exp3 covert noise 23 dyads; Exp4 betting incentives. Equality bias grows with similar sensitivity r=-0.32.
quote: assigned nearly equal weights to each other's opinions regardless of true differences in their competence
limits: Male participants only, perceptual task, small dyads. Exp4 sample size not stated in text read.
agent_relevance: The mirror risk to G4: treating unequal sources as equal peers. Weight by track record, not headcount.

source: Bahrami et al. (2010) Optimally interacting minds (PMC listing only)
finding: Page could not be opened (browser check). Kept as a pointer only: dyads gain over the better member when sensitivities are similar and they share confidence; Mahmoodi 2015 shows the gain shrinks when sensitivities differ.
numbers: not read
limits: Not opened. Do not cite numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: Source of the two-heads-better benefit that holds only when members are similar in skill and independent in noise.

source: Mahmoodi 2015 detail: who arbitrates
finding: Collective benefit depends on who arbitrates. Letting the more sensitive member decide gave a higher collective benefit; weighting error was larger for the less sensitive member.
numbers: t(46)=-4.18 P<0.0004 (benefit); t(46)=4.58 P<1e-4 (weighting error); absolute weighting error vs sensitivity r=-0.29 P<0.004.
limits: Same small samples as b05.
agent_relevance: A judge stronger than the debaters beats a vote of equals; a judge as weak as the debaters adds nothing.

source: Trouche, Johansson, Hall, Mercier (2018) Vigilant conservatism in evaluating communicated information
finding: People weight their own answers more than advice by default, even when a disguised copy of their own answer is shown as the advisor's. Not explained by access to reasons.
numbers: 4 experiments, MTurk, recruited 99/100/50/50. Non-manipulated weight of advice 0.23, 0.20, 0.17, 0.16 (well below 0.5, Exp1 d=1.3). Manipulated 0.39, 0.26, 0.29, 0.22. Detection 23%, 16%, 32%, 26%. Speeded Exp4: no rise in WoA.
quote: conservativeness cannot be explained by rational access to reasons
limits: Life-expectancy estimates only; non-detectors n=76, 84, 33, 37; self-reported detection; 3-20% trials excluded.
agent_relevance: Humans under-use peers. LLMs show the opposite: they over-defer (see b13-b17). A scaffold must correct in the direction the model errs.

source: Meta-analysis of the weight of advice in decision-making (2025)
finding: People move on average 39% toward advice. Advisor quality is the biggest moderator.
numbers: 53 articles, 129 datasets, 17,296 participants, 346 effect sizes. Pooled WOA 0.39 (95% CI 0.37-0.42). High, neutral, low quality: 0.48, 0.37, 0.32. Uncertain estimates 55% vs objective 35% (t(124)=4.10). Age, gender, individualism had no effect.
quote: individuals, on average, adjusted their estimates to be 39% closer to an advised estimate/s
limits: Egger test significant p=0.012, trim-and-fill imputed 8 studies. Only 35% of effects had advice accuracy coded. 111 of 129 samples used computer advisors. Zero movement coded as no weight. Last 47k characters of page not read.
agent_relevance: Human average of 0.39 sits below the 0.5 equal-weight norm. A baseline for how much to move toward a disagreeing peer.

source: Zonca et al. (2026) Adaptive yet suboptimal integration of advice in decision-making
finding: People adapt to advisor accuracy and confidence but under-use good advice, mostly from egocentric bias.
numbers: 89 analyzed (46 Exp1, 43 Exp2). Accuracy 42% to 51% with advice. Mean influence 0.36 (SD 0.10) vs 0.5 expected. Observed-minus-optimal B=-0.16 (CI -0.19 to -0.14). Confidence differences moved influence (B=0.28) though they did not predict accuracy.
quote: the bottleneck is not ignorance but flawed information processing
limits: Only the first 100000 characters read; Exp2 results not confirmed. Artificial advisers, simple perceptual task.
agent_relevance: Confidence difference swayed people even when it did not predict accuracy: do not let a peer's stated confidence set the weight.

source: Wang, Wang, Su, Tong, Song (2024) Rethinking the Bounds of LLM Reasoning: Are Multi-Agent Discussions the Key?
finding: A single agent with a strong prompt (one demonstration) matches the best multi-agent discussion. Discussion helps only without demonstrations. Most common discussion error: wrong answer propagation.
numbers: ChatGPT-3.5 averages over ECQA, GSM8K, FOLIO-wiki: single agent 67.41 direct / 75.63 with demo; MAD(3) 63.42 / 70.04; Debate(3) 71.67 / 73.88; Debate(6) 69.38 / 72.26; CMD(6) 70.75 / 74.46. GSM8K with demo: single 83 vs MAD 78.
limits: ChatGPT-3.5 era models. Small test subsets (about 100 per task).
agent_relevance: With a good task prompt, talking among samples adds nothing and can hurt. Spend budget on the prompt first.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Without oracle labels, self-correction lowers accuracy. Multi-agent debate does not beat self-consistency at equal numbers of responses.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 (round 1) and 41.8 (round 2); GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 and 74.7. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 and 89.0. GSM8K: self-consistency 3 responses 82.5, 6: 85.3, 9: 88.2; debate round 2 (6 responses) 83.2, round 3 (9 responses) 83.0; debate round 1 with 3 responses 76.7. GPT-3.5 kept its first answer 74.7% of the time on GSM8K and changed correct to wrong more often than wrong to correct.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning
limits: Oracle-label setups (GSM8K GPT-3.5 75.9 to 84.3 area, GPT-4 95.5 to 97.5) are not real self-correction.
agent_relevance: Debate rounds are not a substitute for independent samples. Count calls fairly against voting.

source: Du, Li, Torralba, Tenenbaum, Mordatch (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
finding: The founding claim: 3 agents, 2 rounds of debate beat single agent, reflection and majority vote on several tasks.
numbers: Arithmetic: single 67.0, reflection 72.1, majority 69.0, debate 81.8. GSM8K: 77.0, 75.0, 81.0, 85.0. Chess pawn score: 91.4, 102.1, 102.2, 122.9. Biographies single 66.0, reflection 68.3, debate 73.8; MMLU single 63.9, reflection 57.7, debate 71.1. Persona agents on MMLU 71.1 to 74.2.
limits: About 100 problems per task, GPT-3.5 era, wide error bars (arithmetic majority 69.0 +/- 4.6). Later work (b11, b13, b14, b15) does not reproduce the margin against equal-budget voting.
agent_relevance: The result G4 must be weighed against: the gain over majority vote is real in this paper but small and not robust.

source: Smit, Grinsztajn, Duckworth, Barrett, Pretorius (2024) Should we be going MAD? (ICML 2024)
finding: MAD protocols do not reliably outperform self-consistency or ensembling with multiple reasoning paths. They are sensitive to hyperparameters; tuning the agreement level lifted some above all non-debate baselines.
numbers: Benchmarks of cost, time and accuracy on multiple-choice Q&A (medical and others). Medprompt, Ensemble Refinement and Self-Consistency sit near the top of accuracy at lower cost. Exact table numbers not extracted.
limits: Only abstract, intro and cost-accuracy figure read; accuracy table not extracted.
agent_relevance: Tuning the amount of agreement agents show is a lever (G4: agreement is a hint). Default MAD is not a safe gain.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Across 5 MAD methods, 9 benchmarks, 4 models, MAD mostly fails to beat chain-of-thought or self-consistency. Model heterogeneity improves MAD.
numbers: 36 configurations. Overall for the first method: better than CoT 13.9%, comparable 44.4%, worse 41.7%. Society of Mind below CoT on all 9 datasets with GPT-4o-mini. AgentVerse beat CoT only on MMLU with Claude-3.5-haiku (+0.85%); others at least -3.60%. Heter-SoM +6.4% over SoM-average, Heter-EoT +8.2% over EoT-average, Heter-SoM +5.8% vs CoT-average.
quote: MAD often fail to outperform simple single-agent baselines such as Chain-of-Thought and Self-Consistency
limits: Heterogeneity tested with two models; compared against the average of the two models, not the better one. Cost not equalized in every comparison.
agent_relevance: Supports no persona voters, no debate by default, and mixing different models as the one diversity that helps.

source: Choi, Zhu, Li (2025) Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent LLMs? (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: Majority voting alone gives most of MAD's gain. Theory: debate is a martingale on belief in the correct answer, so debate alone does not raise expected correctness.
numbers: 7 benchmarks, 5 agents. Qwen2.5-7B average: single 0.7205, majority vote 0.7691, best Decentralized MAD (T=2) 0.7377, Centralized MAD 0.6551-0.6672. Llama3.1-8B average: single 0.6203, vote 0.7242, Decentralized T=2 0.6929, Centralized 0.5670-0.6094. Arithmetics Qwen: vote 0.99 vs single 0.814 vs MAD T=5 0.67.
quote: debate alone does not improve expected correctness
limits: Small open models (7-8B), with 32B and GPT-4 checks in appendix. Oracle variant not deployable.
agent_relevance: Strongest support for G4: use independent samples and vote; if debating, bias updates toward evidence, not toward the crowd.

source: Choi, Zhu, Li (2025) interventions that bias the belief update
finding: Letting correct answers keep influence helps. MAD-oracle (true answer favoured) is an upper bound. Realistic variants that follow the previous majority recover part of it.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B averages (T=2): MAD-vanilla 0.7332, Conformist 0.7625, Follower 0.7629, oracle 0.8236. Formal Logic T=5: 0.5000 to 0.6825 with oracle.
limits: Conformist and Follower use the majority of the previous round, so they approximate voting. Oracle needs the true answer.
agent_relevance: Having agents defer to the prior majority recovers voting-level accuracy; real gains need a verifier.

source: Wynn, Satija, Hadfield (2025) Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Debate can reduce accuracy even when stronger models outnumber weaker ones. Models flip from correct to incorrect to agree with peers. A correctness-payoff prompt did not fix it.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B; 100 questions, 5 seeds. Single agent: CSQA 74.8, 57.0, 41.6; MMLU 82.6, 55.6, 34.0; GSM8K 93.2, 76.4, 34.2. Losses after debate up to 9.2 points (MMLU), 12.0 for a 3-model mixed group on MMLU (40.0 to 28.0). Some GSM8K groups gained (up to +4.4). Flip to wrong most likely when the agent was alone in its answer.
quote: models frequently shift from correct to incorrect answers in response to peer reasoning, favoring agreement
limits: Small samples, three tasks, three models. Payoff prompt gave no significant gain.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for conformity in LLM peer panels. Agreement counts must not drive updates (G4).

source: Yao et al. (2025) Peacemaker or Troublemaker: How Sycophancy Shapes Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Higher debater sycophancy goes with disagreement collapse and lower accuracy than single-agent baselines. A peacemaker plus troublemaker pair did best in decentralized debate. A centralized judge was insensitive to its own sycophancy level.
numbers: CommonsenseQA two-agent Qwen vs Qwen: accuracy 81.98% to 83.87% across 45 persona settings, lowest with both peacemakers. Qwen3-32B vs Llama3-70B: 78.95% to 82.06% across 81 settings, best when both troublemakers. About 10% of cases moved from positive disagreement to positive agreement after debate.
limits: Few models and two benchmarks seen; persona prompts set the sycophancy level. Gains from sycophancy control were marginal for same-model pairs.
agent_relevance: Persona effects are small for same-model pairs and larger for different models. Do not rely on persona prompts to rescue same-model panels (G4).

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models (ICLR 2024)
finding: When challenged with 'I don't think that's right. Are you sure?', assistants often drop right answers and falsely admit mistakes, even when the first answer was confident.
numbers: Accuracy drops by up to 27% (Claude 1.3) averaged over six datasets. Models change the initial answer 32% (GPT-4) to 86% (Claude 1.3) and admit a mistake 42% (GPT-4) to 98% (Claude 1.3).
quote: Claude 1.3 wrongly admits mistakes on 98% of questions
limits: User-challenge setting, not peer-model setting; 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Deference to a stated disagreement is a trained habit. A disagreeing sample from another run can trigger the same habit.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg (2025) Correlated Errors in Large Language Models (ICML 2025)
finding: Different LLMs repeat each other's wrong answers far more than chance. More accurate models share errors more. Same provider, base architecture and size add correlation.
numbers: 349 LLMs on 12,032 multiple-choice questions (HuggingFace), 71 LLMs on 14,042 (HELM), 20 LLMs on 1,800 resume pairs. Agreement when both wrong: mean 0.423 on HuggingFace and about 0.60 on HELM, versus a random baseline of 1/3 on HELM. Llama-3.2-90b-vision vs Llama-3.1-70b: 0.97. One pair with no stated link agreed on 0.9987 of questions both missed.
quote: models agree 60% of the time when both models err
limits: Multiple-choice and one hiring task. Chance baseline depends on option count.
agent_relevance: Even different models are not independent peers. Mixing models gives less independence than assumed.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Correlated Errors: LLM-as-judge consequence
finding: A judge model systematically inflates the measured accuracy of models less accurate than itself, because both give the same wrong answer.
numbers: Judges were the most accurate model within a provider (HELM) or architecture; inflation (judged minus true accuracy) is above 0 for weaker models and below 0 for stronger ones.
limits: Judge answer used as stand-in for ground truth. Exact inflation sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: Never grade a model's sample with another sample of the same family as truth.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning (ICLR 2023)
finding: Independent sampling plus majority vote raises accuracy. The reference point for what the independence assumption buys.
numbers: Absolute gains: GSM8K +17.9%, SVAMP +11.0%, AQuA +12.2%, StrategyQA +6.4%, ARC-challenge +3.9%. +3% to +6% for UL2-20B but +9% to +23% for LaMDA-137B; +12% to +18% for PaLM-540B.
limits: Gains shrink on tasks with few repeated answers or when errors are correlated.
agent_relevance: Core of the scaffold's safe aggregation: vote independent samples, treat agreement as a hint.

source: Li et al. (2024) More Agents Is All You Need (TMLR)
finding: Sampling-and-voting scales with the number of agents. Smaller models with more samples reach larger models. Gain grows with task difficulty.
numbers: GSM8K: Llama2-13B at ensemble size 15 reaches Llama2-70B single-sample accuracy; Llama2-70B at 15 and GPT-3.5-Turbo at 20 reach comparable accuracy. Ensemble size up to 40; with Debate limited to 10 for cost.
quote: The accuracy increases with ensemble size across Llama2-13B, Llama2-70B and GPT-3.5-Turbo in GSM8K
limits: Numbers taken from figure captions and intro only. Gain depends on task difficulty.
agent_relevance: Cheap independent samples are the safe use of compute.

source: Hegazy (2024) Diversity of Thought Elicits Stronger Reasoning in Multi-Agent Debate Frameworks
finding: Debating different models beat debating copies of one model.
numbers: After 4 rounds, Gemini-Pro + Mixtral 7Bx8 + PaLM 2-M scored 91% on GSM8K, above GPT-4; 3 copies of Gemini-Pro reached 82%. ASDiv 94%.
limits: Single author, small venue, only abstract and intro read; not independently replicated.
agent_relevance: Same-model peers are the weak case; heterogeneity is the lever, and a single-model scaffold cannot buy it.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: An ensemble of 12 different LLMs matched a crowd of 925 human forecasters. Showing the human median to a model improved it, but averaging was better.
numbers: 31 binary questions. LLM crowd Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs no-information 0.25, t(30)=-2.35 p=0.026; human crowd 0.19 (SD 0.19), difference p=0.850. Equivalence bound 0.081. Single models: GPT-4 0.15, Claude 2 0.21, Llama-2-70B 0.25. Exposure to human median improved accuracy 17%-28%. Mean model prediction 57.35 (above 50).
limits: Only 31 questions; acquiescence bias; the crowd was 12 distinct models, not samples of one.
agent_relevance: Aggregation across different models works; averaging with outside information beat letting one model absorb it.

source: Schoenegger, Park et al. (2024) AI-Augmented Predictions: LLM Assistants Improve Human Forecasting Accuracy
finding: Human forecasters who consulted a frontier LLM assistant were more accurate, including a deliberately noisy overconfident assistant.
numbers: N=991, six forecasting questions. Accuracy up 24% to 28% vs control. Without one outlier item: 41% for the superforecasting assistant, 29% for the noisy one.
limits: One outlier item drove part of the effect. Abstract and intro only; the diversity-loss analysis was not read.
agent_relevance: Even a poor advisor can help a human; a model's own noisy samples do not carry the same independence.
